sections.h2: Selling a house in Springfield Township
sections.html:
Springfield here means Springfield Township in Delaware County, a suburb of single-family homes southwest of Philadelphia with the 19064 ZIP code. Plenty of Pennsylvania townships share the name, so check that your buyer, your title agent and your paperwork all point to the Delaware County one. Any buyer faces the same three stops: a township resale inspection, paid-up tax bills and a deed recorded in Media.

Many Springfield houses date from the postwar building boom, and original layouts and aging mechanicals are common. Expect questions about the roof, furnace and basement at every showing.

Population is 25,039, almost level with the 2020 count of 25,070. Owners live in 93.8 percent of homes, which is very high, and the middle owned home is valued at $414,900. Households average 2.87 people and 24.2 percent of residents are under 18, which points to family buyers who want room near the city.

With so few rentals, investor-owned houses are a small slice of the market. If you rented your house out at any point, landlords file a Business Privilege Rental Tax Return with the township. Ask the tax office which filings you need to close before settlement.

The township offers a Resale Inspection Appointment Request on its homepage, which tells you a sale brings the code office to your door. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, and ask what the inspector will check, what it costs and how long a certificate stays valid.

The code office publishes the violations it sees most often. They make a handy walk-through list before you put a sign in the yard:

  • Grass cannot grow higher than 8 inches.
  • Plantings at an intersection can be no taller than 18 inches, and shrubs cannot block signs or signals.
  • House numbers must be 4 inches high and visible from the street.
  • Vehicles may park only on paved surfaces, never on the lawn.
  • Owners maintain the curbs and sidewalks in front of the property, and snow comes off public sidewalks within 24 hours after it stops falling.
  • Trash containers stay behind the front building line and come off the street within 12 hours of pickup.

Repair permits are filed on the township's OpenGov portal. Call the inspector with questions, and keep the paperwork for any large repair, since it is much easier to defend work that has a permit on file.

sections.h2: When are township and school taxes due?
sections.html:
Two bills arrive each year on separate calendars. If your parcel still owes money when you sell, the closing agent pays it from your proceeds.

Springfield Township and Springfield School District billing windows
BillBilling date2% discount throughFace amount10% penalty after
Township tax, sewer, refuseFebruary 1March 31April 1 to May 31June 1
School tax (fiscal year July 1 to June 30)July 1August 31September 1 to October 31November 1

Sewer rent and refuse ride on the township bill, and sewer rent is figured from last year's water use. A sewer or refuse balance left unpaid becomes a lien. Real estate tax that stays unpaid goes to the Tax Claim Bureau in Media by the following January. The township tax office is at 610-544-1300.

Homes with an approved homestead may pay school tax in three installments, and the township's collection books close on December 31. Phone the tax office a few weeks ahead for your parcel's exact figure.

sections.h2: Transfer tax and recording in Delaware County
sections.html:
A transfer here costs 2 percent of the price, with one point going to Harrisburg and one to the township. Four places pay more under county rules: Radnor, Upper Darby, Upper Providence and Chester City. Springfield is not one of them, so the ordinary rate applies to your sale.

Pennsylvania makes both parties answerable for the tax, but your contract picks who actually writes the check. Put that choice on paper in the agreement of sale, and expect the title company to gather the money when you sign.

The Recorder of Deeds sits in Room 108 at Government Center, 201 W. Front Street, Media, and answers at 610-891-4152. The office will not draft your deed or search your title for you, and the only liens in its files are mortgages. Once your loan is paid off the lender files a mortgage satisfaction, which you can confirm later on the county's public access site.

sections.h2: What happens between contract and closing?
sections.html:
Most sales here follow the same order. First comes the agreement of sale, then the buyer's title search, then the inspector's visit. Open tax balances, sewer and refuse charges and any mortgage payoff are then totaled by the closing agent.

  • Request your tax balances from the township tax office a few weeks before the settlement date.
  • Get a payoff letter from your lender and locate your deed.
  • Fix the violations from the checklist above so the inspection does not push back the closing.
  • Confirm the transfer tax split in writing.

On settlement day you sign the deed, the closing agent subtracts liens and unpaid taxes from what you receive, and the paperwork travels to Media. Cash buyers have no lender appraisal to wait on, so their closings can come sooner, yet the township inspection and your tax bills still apply.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html:
A short folder saves days later. Buyers, lenders and the title agent all ask for the same few items, and several come from township offices that answer by phone during business hours.

  • Your most recent township and school tax bills, plus a call to the tax office at 610-544-1300 for current balances.
  • Any permit records for decks, finished basements, roofs or other repairs, since the code office may ask for them during the resale inspection.
  • Sewer and refuse account details, because those charges ride on the township bill.
  • If you ever rented the house, proof that your Business Privilege Rental Tax Return filings are closed out.

Inherited the place? Find out from the estate's lawyer who may sign the deed before an offer is accepted.

Listing with an agent works well for a house in good shape. Clearing the violations above before it goes live keeps the resale inspection from delaying your closing date.

If the house needs work or time is short, a sale straight to an investor or cash buyer removes the bank's approval step and most arguments over repairs. Whichever door you pick, ask for price, closing day and transfer tax duty in writing. Then set each offer next to the amount a listing would put in your pocket after commissions and repairs.

faqs.q: Which county records a Springfield, PA deed?
faqs.a: Delaware County. The Recorder of Deeds works from the Government Center in Media. Deeds and mortgages get recorded there, normally by the closing agent on your behalf.

faqs.q: What transfer tax would a Springfield sale carry?
faqs.a: Two percent, split evenly between the state and the municipality. Springfield is not on the county's higher-rate list.

faqs.q: Do I need a resale inspection to sell in Springfield Township?
faqs.a: Plan on one. The township offers a Resale Inspection Appointment Request on its homepage. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, for the current checklist and fees before you list.

faqs.q: When is the Springfield school tax discount?
faqs.a: School bills go out July 1. Pay by August 31 and you get 2 percent off. Face amount is due September 1 to October 31, and the 10 percent penalty begins November 1.

faqs.q: What happens to unpaid sewer and refuse charges when I sell?
faqs.a: They become liens against the property, so they must be cleared. Phone the township tax office for the balance, and the title company will pay it at settlement.
